planting.note: Plant the fleshy-rooted bulbs 4-5 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil; Juno irises have brittle storage roots attached below the bulb that snap easily, so handle and plant them with care.

directions: Plant the fragile, finger-like bulbs in late summer or early fall in full sun and very sharply drained, gritty soil, since Juno irises rot quickly if the ground stays wet during their required summer baking. In early spring each stem carries several orchid-like, pale yellow and white flowers low among glossy, channeled leaves that clasp the stalk. Native to the rocky, dry slopes of Central Asia, it is best suited to raised beds, bulb frames, or rock gardens that can be kept dry after bloom. Avoid disturbing the clump once established, as the swollen storage roots resent transplanting.

subcategory: wild species iris - bulbous Xiphium group

planting.note: Plant true bulbs 3-4 inches deep in warm, free-draining soil; this wild parent of the Dutch iris hybrids is less cold-hardy than bearded irises and benefits from a sheltered, sunny site.

directions: Set true bulbs in fall in full sun and light, free-draining soil that warms quickly in spring; in colder zones lift and store the bulbs over winter as you would with its Dutch iris hybrid descendants. Slender stems carry smaller, more delicate flowers than bearded iris in shades of blue, purple, yellow, or white in late spring, with narrow grassy foliage. Native to the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa, it is one of the two wild bulbous species (along with Iris latifolia) behind the florist Dutch iris trade. Grow in a warm border or raised bed where summer drainage is assured.

subcategory: wild species iris - bulbous Xiphium group

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in cool, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil; unlike its relative Iris xiphium, this Pyrenean species tolerates damper summers and heavier soil.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in sun and cool, humus-rich soil that holds some summer moisture, since this species comes from damp alpine meadows of the Pyrenees rather than the dry Mediterranean habitats of most bulbous irises. Despite the common name, it is not native to England but naturalized so successfully in Lancashire bulb fields that it picked up the name 'English iris.' Large, broad-petaled violet-blue to white flowers without the yellow throat markings typical of Spanish iris open in early summer, later than most bulbous irises. Good for cottage borders and cooler, slightly moister rock gardens than Iris xiphium requires.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in sharply drained, lime-rich or neutral soil in full sun; a true miniature best suited to rock gardens, troughs, or an alpine house.

directions: Plant the small bulbs in fall in full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil, since this rock-dwelling Portuguese daffodil needs a dry, baked summer rest to flower well the following year. Short, rush-like foliage accompanies dainty stems each bearing one to three small, bright yellow, fragrant flowers in early to mid spring. It grows naturally on limestone and schist outcrops near the Tagus valley, making it well suited to raised beds, troughs, and alpine collections rather than open borders. Give it the same sharp-drainage treatment as other miniature jonquil-group species.

planting.note: Plant tiny bulbs about 2 inches deep in sharply drained, gritty soil; often grown in pots or an alpine house in regions with cold, wet winters.

directions: Plant the very small bulbs in fall in full sun and sharply drained, gritty soil, giving this dwarf Portuguese species the same hot, dry summer dormancy it gets on its native schist slopes. Tiny, deep golden-yellow flowers with a distinctively ruffled, rolled perianth open just one to four per stem over grass-fine leaves in early spring. Its diminutive scale and need for reliable drainage make it a favorite for alpine houses, troughs, and raised scree beds rather than general garden use. In climates with wet winters, growing it in a pot under glass protects the bulbs from rot.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained soil in sun to light shade; tolerates lightly wooded sites better than most ornamental onions.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 3 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun or light shade, where it will slowly form drifts at the edge of borders or beneath deciduous shrubs. Loose, open umbels of pure white, star-shaped flowers appear on slender stems in late spring above narrow, grassy, gray-green leaves. Native to the limestone hills around Mount Lebanon, it is one of the more woodland-tolerant wild onions and combines well with other spring bulbs without the strong onion scent some alliums carry when bruised. Leave clumps undisturbed to bulk up and self-seed over several seasons.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; a scree or rock garden plant from the southern Alps.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil, mimicking the rocky scree slopes of the southern Alps where this species grows wild. In early summer, wiry stems nod under loose clusters of large, bell-shaped, deep rosy-pink flowers with notably broad petal segments, held above a few flat, strap-shaped leaves. It closely resembles the more widely grown Allium narcissiflorum but opens slightly earlier with wider, more flared flowers. Best in a rock garden, raised bed, or scree planting where its dry-summer requirements can be met.
